chapter: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
title: Arnold Wright, the Kentucky State innovator, and the Shirley Horn date
summary: Arnold Wright set up band scholarships at Alabama State and Kentucky State, became friends with Jones's father, and met John Levy at a record date.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Tell me about Arnold Wright. You said he was a social science teacher at Kentucky State.
Uh-huh.
But he was the one responsible for bringing the band in, Danny Williams' band in, and you said he'd done something similar before with -- some kind of involvement with Erskine Hawkins. What was that?

That was at Alabama State. Erskine Hawkins's band, it was the Alabama State Collegians, and I thought it was a very nice setup. It's like football players would get scholarships, but you have to work on the campus, if you don't have the money or something, you know, if your family doesn't have the money to pay your way through. And that was the setup that we had, you know?

But Arnold Wright, what kind of a man was he? Was he involved in music in any way? The fact that he set these programs up in two different colleges, he sounds like quite an innovator and a real friend to music.
Yes, he was. He was definitely an

innovator and a friend of music, and he had these ideas and it broadened the campus attitude. Not only did they know about football, basketball and everything else, but they had their own school band there. They'd play all the proms and play other colleges, you know. He and my father became very friendly, because he kind of took over for -- what was I, about 17 years old, I guess, and my father and I, we were getting to -- my mother had just passed, and I said, "Well, I guess Pops needs another lady," you know, and he eventually did get one. But this was a great turn in the road for me, and it was great for my father too at that point, you know? And Arnold Wright and my father became good friends.
He didn't -- was he a musician at all? I mean he wasn't a music teacher, he was a social science teacher. I wondered how he got involved in music. Do you know?
He just loved it.
I see.

That's the only thing I can say, he just loved it. In fact the last time I saw him was in New York and I was doing a recording date with a singer named Shirley Horne. It was a big string date, you know, we had about 20 strings or so. And Arnold Wright came to the record date. He was visiting in New York, you know. And he knew of John Levy and John Levy was in the booth producing the date. So Arnold Wright looked at me -- oh, this was years later, a generation
later I guess, and he says, "Whatever happened to that fellow John Levy?" I said, "You've been sitting next to him for the last two hours."
(Laughter)
That's the same John Levy. And, oh, we had a wonderful time. And he used to always say, "Jones, don't get depressed about your industry, because it's a very important thing to American culture."
Did he keep his affiliation with music programs even after the days of the Collegians?
Oh, I think that -- yes. Because I have a letter -- I think we looked at it in a book, where they want me to do something there with the music department, you know.
But is Mr. Wright still there?
Yeah, Mr. Wright's still there. I guess he's a senior citizen teacher now, you know.
Uh-huh.
He's along in years, but he's done his work in his peak years, you know. He was an innovator. He got it started.
